When I was 16, in my first year of high school, something happened to me that I didn't remember again for almost 10 years. One winter evening, I was taking the bus home after staying late at school. A friend and I were the last passengers, chatting and joking with the driver. We'd ridden with him before. My friend got off before me, leaving me alone with him. The driver offered to drop me closer to home instead of at the regular stop. When we got there, he said, "Come here, give me a hug. It was nice talking to you." I was 16. I trusted him. It never crossed my mind that a man in his 50s or 60s asking a teenage girl for a hug might have other intentions. So I hugged him. I felt his hands go under my jacket, under my shirt, and onto my breasts. I froze. I remember him saying, "[name], nothing's happening. [name] happening." I don't remember whether I pulled away or he let me go. I just remember getting out of that bus. I never took one of those private buses again. To this day, I can't remember his face. But I remember the fear. The alternative transport cost about three times as much, and my parents didn't have much money. They gave me money for the bus, and I secretly used my pocket money to cover the difference because I didn't want to tell them why. At 16, I was spending my own money just to make sure I'd never be alone with a bus driver again. That night, I stopped crying before I walked through the door. I told no one. Somehow my mind buried it for almost a decade. When the memory came back in my late twenties, I couldn't even tell my sister out loud. I had to write it down. For years, part of me thought I'd been stupid and naive. I know better now. I was a 16-year-old girl who trusted an adult. He was the adult who chose to sexually assault a child. That responsibility was his, not mine. Nothing "worse" happened that night. I know I was luckier than many girls. But that doesn't mean it left no scars. Even now, when I hear stories about girls being abused or assaulted by older men they trusted, I remember that bus. I don't remember his face, but more than 20 years later, I remember what he did. I guess this is one of the demons I carry. That's my story.
